info.title: Disaster Response Coordination Platform
info.description:
Backend for coordinating disaster response: incident records, automatic location
resolution from free text, geospatial resource search, aggregated community
reports, and a live event stream.

### Getting started

1. `POST /api/v1/auth/login` with `{"username": "admin", "password": "admin123"}`
2. Click **Authorize** above and paste the `access_token`
3. `POST /api/v1/disasters` - omit the coordinates and let the service resolve
   the location from your description

### Demo accounts

| username | role | permissions |
|---|---|---|
| `admin` | admin | full access, including `DELETE` |
| `contributor` | contributor | create; update **only their own** records |
| `responder` | responder | read-only |

### Things worth looking at

* **Geospatial** - `GET /disasters/{id}/resources` uses PostGIS `ST_DWithin`
  against a GiST-indexed `geography(Point, 4326)` column.
* **Caching** - `GET /disasters/{id}/reports` returns `X-Cache: HIT|MISS|STALE`.
* **Failure handling** - stop the mock provider
  (`docker compose stop mock-services`) and re-request reports: you get a `200`
  with `degraded: true`, not a `500`.
* **Real-time** - `curl -N http://localhost:8000/api/v1/events/stream`, then
  create a disaster in another terminal.

get.description:
Check every dependency and report per-component status.

Returns 503 when a hard dependency is down, so an orchestrator or load
balancer can act on the status code alone without parsing the body.

The cache is a **soft** dependency: with ``CACHE_ALLOW_MEMORY_FALLBACK`` the
app still serves correctly without Redis, just without a shared cache or
cross-worker events. It is reported as degraded, not failed.

Convenience endpoint for exploring the demo.

Authentication is required, and only public fields are returned - no hashes.
A real system would restrict this to admins; it is open to any authenticated
caller here purely so a reviewer can see the seeded roles.

get.description:
Resources within ``radius_km`` of a point, nearest first.

**How the search works.** The radius filter is a PostGIS
``ST_DWithin(location, point, radius_km * 1000)`` against a
``geography(Point, 4326)`` column with a **GiST index**. ``ST_DWithin`` is
index-accelerated: the planner uses the index to discard rows by bounding
box first and computes exact distances only on the survivors.
``ST_Distance(...) < r`` would look equivalent and force a full table scan.

Distances come back from the database in kilometres, and ordering happens in
SQL so ``LIMIT`` returns the genuinely nearest rows rather than the first N
matches re-sorted in Python.

**Search centre.** Supply ``lat``/``lng`` to search around an arbitrary
point (a responder's own position). Omit them and the disaster's own resolved
location is used. If the disaster has no location and none is given, the
response is a 422 - "we do not know where to look" is not the same answer as
"there is nothing nearby".

**Radius cap.** ``radius_km`` is capped at ``MAX_RADIUS_KM`` so one request
cannot be used to scan the whole table.

parameters.name: lat

schema.description: Search centre latitude. Defaults to the disaster's own.

parameters.description: Search centre latitude. Defaults to the disaster's own.

post.description:
Register a resource.

**Authorization:** ``admin`` only. Resources are reference data that the
whole response depends on - a wrong shelter location sends people to the
wrong place - so writes are deliberately narrower than for incidents.

Coordinates are required here, unlike on a disaster: a resource with no
position can never be returned by a proximity search.

get.summary: Community and official reports for a disaster
get.description:
Aggregated reports from two external providers.

**Sources.** A mock social-media feed and a mock official bulletin feed, each
running as a separate service behind a real HTTP boundary. Their payload
shapes differ and are normalised into one ``Report`` model, so adding or
swapping a provider changes only its client.

**Caching.** Responses are cached for ``CACHE_TTL_REPORTS`` (default 5
minutes) in Redis, fronted by a short in-process tier. The ``X-Cache`` header
and ``meta.cache`` report ``HIT``, ``MISS`` or ``STALE``, and
``meta.age_seconds`` gives the age of the underlying data. Pass
``?refresh=true`` to force a re-fetch.

**Failure handling.** Providers are called concurrently, and each one's
outcome appears in ``meta.sources`` as ``ok``, ``empty``, ``failed`` or
``circuit_open``:

* one provider down -> the other's reports are still returned,
  ``meta.degraded = true``, and the partial result is cached only briefly
  so recovery is picked up quickly;
* both down, something cached -> the cached payload is served with
  ``X-Cache: STALE`` and ``meta.degraded = true``. A responder is far better
  served by five-minute-old reports than by an error;
* both down, nothing cached -> 502, the only case where this endpoint fails.

**Prioritisation.** Each report is scored by a deterministic, explainable
classifier into ``critical``/``high``/``medium``/``low``, with
``matched_signals`` listing the rules that fired. Results are sorted most
urgent first.

post.description:
Create an incident.

**Location resolution.** If ``latitude``/``longitude`` are omitted, the
service infers the location from ``description`` - extracting a place name
and geocoding it. Explicit coordinates always win, and the resolution method
is reported back in ``location.source`` with a ``location.confidence`` score.

Resolution never blocks the write: if nothing can be resolved, the incident
is still created with ``location.point = null``.

**Authorization:** ``admin`` or ``contributor``.

**Emits:** ``disaster_created`` on the real-time channel.

get.description:
List incidents.

Filters combine with AND. Supplying ``lat``/``lng``/``radius_km`` restricts
results to incidents whose resolved location falls inside the radius, using
the same PostGIS ``ST_DWithin`` path as the nearby-resources search, and adds
a ``distance_km`` to each item.

This endpoint is public (no token needed) so the map demo can render without
credentials. Every write endpoint is authenticated.

patch.description:
Update an incident. Only the fields present in the body are changed.

**Authorization:** ``admin`` may update any record; ``contributor`` may
update **only records they created** - a 403 otherwise. This is the
ownership rule the brief asks to be demonstrated, and it is enforced in the
service layer where the record is loaded.

**Location.** Changing ``description`` re-runs resolution unless explicit
coordinates are supplied in the same request. Pass
``"reresolve_location": true`` to force it.

**Emits:** ``disaster_updated``, carrying the list of changed fields.

delete.description:
Delete an incident.

**Authorization:** ``admin`` only - the second half of the demonstrated
authorization rule. A contributor receives 403 even for their own record,
because deletion destroys shared situational awareness in a way that editing
does not.

Returns 204 with no body, and records the deletion in the audit log.

**Emits:** ``disaster_deleted``.

get.description: Who changed this incident, what they changed, and when.

get.summary: Server-Sent Events stream of disaster events
get.description:
Subscribe to live events over SSE.

Verify it with::

    curl -N http://localhost:8000/api/v1/events/stream

then create or update a disaster in another terminal and watch the event
arrive. A ``: heartbeat`` comment line is emitted every 20s to keep
intermediaries from closing an idle connection.

example.description: Heavy flooding has affected Manhattan, NYC. Several subway stations are submerged.
example.title: Manhattan Flash Flooding

DisasterUpdate.title: DisasterUpdate
DisasterUpdate.description:
PATCH body. Every field optional; absent means "leave unchanged".

``exclude_unset`` at the call site is what distinguishes "not provided" from
"explicitly set to null" - which is why partial update needs its own model
rather than a create model with defaults.

geojson.title: Geojson
geojson.description: GeoJSON representation, for clients that want to feed a map directly.

GeoPoint.title: GeoPoint
GeoPoint.description:
A resolved coordinate pair.

Exposed as explicit ``latitude``/``longitude`` rather than a GeoJSON
``[lng, lat]`` array. GeoJSON's longitude-first ordering is a notorious
source of transposed-coordinate bugs; named fields make the mistake
impossible for an API consumer to make silently.

source.title: Source
source.description: How the location was derived: llm+nominatim, rules+nominatim, rules+gazetteer, manual, or unresolved

LocationInfo.title: LocationInfo
LocationInfo.description:
Resolved location plus its provenance.

``source`` and ``confidence`` travel with the coordinates so a consumer can
decide how much to trust them. An inferred point and a human-entered point
are not interchangeable when you are dispatching a rescue team.

center_source.title: Center Source
center_source.description: 'query' if supplied by the caller, else 'disaster'

NearbySearchResponse.title: NearbySearchResponse
NearbySearchResponse.description:
Echoes the effective search parameters alongside the results.

The centre point may have been derived from the disaster rather than sent by
the caller, so returning it removes any ambiguity about what was searched.

total.title: Total
total.description: Total rows matching the filter, ignoring pagination

ProblemDetail.title: ProblemDetail
ProblemDetail.description: RFC 9457 error body. Declared so it appears in the OpenAPI document.

ReadinessStatus.title: ReadinessStatus
ReadinessStatus.description:
Readiness is about dependencies; liveness is about the process.

Kept separate so an orchestrator restarts a hung process but merely stops
routing traffic to an instance whose database is briefly unreachable.

matched_signals.title: Matched Signals
matched_signals.description: Which rules fired. Present so the ranking is auditable rather than an opaque score.

Report.title: Report
Report.description:
One normalised community or official report.

Every provider gets flattened into this. The mock social service returns
``{content, user, created_at}``; the official bulletin feed returns
``{headline, body, issued_at, agency}``. Normalising at the boundary means
the rest of the system never branches on provider.

example.author: citizen123
example.content: Need drinking water near Manhattan, we have been without since 6am

ReportPriority.title: ReportPriority
ReportPriority.description: Triage bucket assigned by the classifier (see services/classification.py).

degraded.title: Degraded
degraded.description: True when at least one provider failed and cached or fallback data was served instead

sources.title: Sources
sources.description: Per-provider outcome: ok | cached | failed | circuit_open

ReportsMeta.title: ReportsMeta
ReportsMeta.description:
Everything the caller needs to judge how much to trust this payload.

A degraded response returns 200, not 502: stale reports are far more useful
to a responder than an error page. But it must say so, loudly and in-band -
silently serving stale data as if it were live would be the actual failure.

distance_km.title: Distance Km
distance_km.description: Great-circle distance from the query point, kilometres

ResourceType.description: Kinds of response resource. The brief names the first five.

UserPublic.title: UserPublic
UserPublic.description:
The only user representation that ever leaves the service.

``password_hash`` is absent by construction rather than stripped on the way
out - a field that does not exist on the response model cannot be leaked by
a future careless change.
